Taste
tāste
v. and n. (rendering Hebrew ta'am, Greek geuomai)
From Old French taster, to handle or try, from Latin taxare, to touch or test — the original sense is to try a thing by handling, then by the tongue. Hebrew ta'am means both to taste and to perceive or discern, and the same noun means good judgment; the Hebrew treats discernment as a palate.

Biblical Definition

Scripture uses taste for the most personal kind of knowledge — not what a man has heard about a thing, but what he has had in his own mouth. The Psalmist's invitation is exactly that: “O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him” (Psalm 34:8). Peter takes the same verse into the new covenant as the ground of an appetite for the word: “If so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious” (1 Peter 2:3). The word is then used for the deepest of all experiences, undergone in the sinner's room by the Son of God: “that he by the grace of God should taste death for every man” (Hebrews 2:9) — not a sip but the cup drained, since to taste death in the Hebrew idiom is to experience it fully. And the same epistle uses the word for a real but not saving acquaintance with divine things: men who “have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost” (Hebrews 6:4) and afterwards fall away. Taste therefore cuts two ways. It is the language of assurance, since a man who has tasted needs no argument that honey is sweet; and it is the language of solemn warning, since a man may taste much and never swallow.

Webster 1828 Definition

To try or perceive by the tongue; to experience for oneself; also discernment or relish. In Scripture, taste and see that the LORD is good; having tasted that the Lord is gracious; Christ tasting death for every man; and those who taste of the heavenly gift and fall away.

expand to see more

TASTE, v.t. 1. To perceive by means of the tongue; to have a sensation excited by something on the tongue.

2. To try by eating a little; to try the relish of.

3. To experience; to feel; to undergo; as, to taste of death.

4. From Old French taster, Latin taxare, to touch, to handle, to try.

5. In Scripture, O taste and see that the LORD is good, Ps. 34; taste death for every man, Heb. 2.

Key Scripture

Psalm 34:8 — "O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him."

1 Peter 2:3 — "If so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious."

Hebrews 2:9 — "But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour; that he by the grace of God should taste death for every man."

Hebrews 6:4 — "For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost,"

Modern Corruption

Religious experience is made self-authenticating, so that having tasted something is taken as proof of conversion; and in reaction, others deny that Christianity is experienced at all and reduce it to assent.

expand to see more

Hebrews 6:4 stands as a permanent rebuke to the assumption that a strong religious experience proves a saved man. The people described there were enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, were made partakers of the Holy Ghost in His common operations, tasted the good word of God and the powers of the world to come — and fell away. Much modern evangelism has no category for them, and so counts every emotional response as a new birth, records the decision, and leaves the man assured of a salvation he never received. The Reformed doctrine of perseverance answers this exactly: those who are truly regenerate persevere, and therefore falling away finally proves that the taste was never eating. “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19). The pastoral use of the text is not to unsettle the weak believer but to press every professor to examine whether he has trusted, not merely tasted.

The opposite error strips the Christian life of experience altogether, making faith a bare assent to propositions with no answering affection. Scripture will not have it. Psalm 34:8 commands a taste; Peter grounds a craving for the sincere milk of the word on having tasted grace; the Psalms are full of a delight that is felt. The Puritans were exact here and worth recovering: they distinguished between the affections wrought by the Spirit in a renewed heart and the transient impressions that common grace can raise in an unrenewed one, and they tested both by fruit and continuance rather than by intensity. Real tasting produces appetite, and appetite produces feeding, and feeding produces growth — and where those do not follow, the taste was a visit, not a home.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ta'am, to taste and to perceive, with the noun meaning both flavour and discretion; Greek geuomai, to taste, and by idiom to experience.

expand to see more

Hebrew ta'am (H2938) — to taste, and thence to perceive or discern; “the mouth tasteth meat” (Job 34:3).

Hebrew ta'am (H2940) — taste, flavour, and also judgment or discretion; the manna tasted as wafers made with honey (Exodus 16:31).

Greek geuomai (G1089) — to taste, to eat, and idiomatically to experience fully; used of tasting death (Hebrews 2:9).

Greek chrēstos (G5543) — gracious, kind; the adjective Peter joins to tasting in 1 Peter 2:3.

Greek metochos (G3353) — a partaker or sharer; used of those made partakers of the Holy Ghost in Hebrews 6:4.

Usage

"Of experimental knowledge of God: O taste and see that the LORD is good (Psalm 34:8)."

"Of Christ's undergoing of death: that he by the grace of God should taste death for every man (Hebrews 2:9)."

"Of a real but unsaving acquaintance: have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost (Hebrews 6:4)."
